newsitem.title: UK: Indonesia succession looms but investors loyal.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia succession looms but investors loyal.

text.p: Foreign investors will continue doing business in Indonesia because of the country's sound economic fundamentals despite uncertainty over who will succeed the long-serving President Suharto, fund managers said.

London-based managers said investor attention had drifted away from political issues after riots in the capital Jakarta in June but added they would again become a focus during general elections in May next year.
Charles Brock, fund manager at Foreign & Colonial Emerging Markets, said he expected Indonesia's capital markets to perform very well in the next six months.

"I think most investors have very short memories," he said. "The underlying story is that companies are still making money, corporate profitability will probably be up 20 percent this year and that the situation is still very good."

Last June, rioters set buildings and vehicles on fire after police stormed the headquarters of the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) and evicted supporters of the ousted opposition leader Megawati Sukarnoputri.
Some Asian-based analysts said it was the issue of the successon that sparked the disturbances. Indonesia's financial markets were battered but share prices recovered as the capital calmed down.
But investors agree that one of the key concerns now for the market is who will succeed the 75-year-old Suharto.
Merrill Lynch said in a report this month that Indonesia's current economic trends were positive and Suharto, who came to power in 1967, would probably be elected for a seventh term.
"The expectations that President Suharto will run again are very strong. It also seems likely that he will win again."
